intro: In Au bord d’une source, the left hand reaches over the right to catch little notes above the running water. Eugen d’Albert, a pupil of Liszt, plays this Swiss miniature on an early Odeon disc.

sections.label: A · Ripples and crossed hands
sections.mNote: Short notes dart above and below the right hand’s semiquavers

sections.label: B · The spring in full flow
sections.mNote: Scales and arpeggios carry the tune across the keyboard

sections.label: A′ · The ripples subside
sections.mNote: The flowing piano writing continues towards the close

cues.title: Hands over running water
cues.text: The right hand plays rippling semiquavers; the left picks out short notes, first underneath them, then two octaves higher. Each crossing catches another glint on the water. Liszt marks the opening Allegretto grazioso, with the melody sweet and tranquil.
cues.evidence: The opening notation and markings are reproduced on IMSLP’s work page: https://imslp.org/wiki/Années_de_pèlerinage_I,_S.160_(Liszt,_Franz). The crossed-hand pattern is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_bord_d%27une_source.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Switzerland with Marie
cues.text: In 1835 Liszt leaves Paris with Marie d’Agoult. They settle in Switzerland, where he teaches at the Geneva Conservatory and their daughter Blandine is born in December. This spring belongs to the Swiss landscapes he later gathers into Années de pèlerinage.
cues.evidence: Liszt chronology, entries for 1835–36: https://www.liszt.org/p/chronology.html. The miniature’s earlier and revised versions are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_bord_d%27une_source.

cues.title: From Glasgow to Weimar
cues.text: D’Albert is born in Glasgow and studies in London under Arthur Sullivan. Still a teenager, he goes to Vienna, stays with the conductor Hans Richter and then joins Liszt’s pupils in Weimar.
cues.evidence: Eliot Levin’s biography gives d’Albert’s Glasgow birth, London training, stay with Richter from late 1881 and subsequent study with Liszt: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/c.asp?c=C6.

cues.title: Scales join the ripples
cues.text: Scales and arpeggios join the melody’s successive appearances. They climb into the piano’s highest reaches, run down again and turn back into the tune. The water keeps moving while the hands change places.
cues.evidence: The account of the piano writing at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_bord_d%27une_source describes the connecting scales and arpeggios, their ascent and descent, and the return to the melody.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: He could fit an orchestra under ten fingers, then end a lifetime at the piano with a few notes left hanging in the air.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces; no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked. A single pianist had taken possession of an entire evening.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained Liszt’s homeland, though German and French were the languages he used most easily. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano; Antonio Salieri taught him composition. Paris followed in 1823, but its Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. Private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha, continued his education.
